title: Diagnose CloudFront 403 Error
description: A user reports receiving a 403 Access Denied error when accessing static assets through CloudFront. Inspect the architecture to find the root cause.

details.label: Note
details.value: OAC requires a bucket policy granting s3:GetObject to the CloudFront service principal

explanation: The S3 bucket policy is missing. When using CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC), the S3 bucket must have a policy that explicitly grants s3:GetObject permission to the CloudFront service principal. Without this policy, S3 denies all requests from CloudFront, resulting in a 403 Access Denied error.

title: Diagnose S3 Access Issue
description: A user cannot download an object from an S3 bucket. Use the AWS CLI simulator to investigate and identify the root cause.
scenario: A developer reports they cannot download objects from the `my-app-bucket` S3 bucket. They receive an AccessDenied error. Use the simulated AWS CLI to run diagnostic commands and determine the root cause.

commands.output: An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the ListObjectsV2 operation: Access Denied
An error occurred (AccessDenied) when calling the ListObjectsV2 operation: Access Denied

answers.text: The IAM user has no S3 permissions
The bucket policy has an explicit Deny on s3:GetObject
The S3 bucket is in a different region

explanation: The bucket policy contains an explicit Deny statement for s3:GetObject on all principals. In AWS IAM, an explicit Deny always overrides any Allow — even if the user has AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess attached. The fix is to remove or modify the Deny statement in the bucket policy.

title: Fix S3 IAM Policy
description: An EC2 instance role cannot read objects from a specific S3 bucket. Fix the IAM policy to grant least-privilege access.
scenario: An EC2 instance needs to read objects from the `my-app-bucket` S3 bucket, but the current IAM policy grants overly broad access using a wildcard Resource. Your task is to fix the policy so it follows least-privilege principles by restricting access to only the `my-app-bucket` bucket.
explanation: The original policy used "Resource": "*" which grants s3:GetObject access to every S3 bucket in the account. Following the principle of least privilege, the Resource should be scoped to only the specific bucket needed: "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-bucket/*". This ensures the EC2 instance can only read objects from my-app-bucket.

title: Build a Highly Available Web Application
description: Design a fault-tolerant web application architecture using AWS services. Place the correct components and connect them properly.
scenario: Design a multi-AZ highly available web application that survives a single AZ failure. Use CDN for edge caching, an autoscaling web tier across AZs behind an ALB, durable object storage for static assets, and a multi-AZ managed database with automated failover.
validationChecks: ALB routes to EC2 instances in multiple AZs
EC2 instances connect to RDS database
explanation: A highly available web application requires CloudFront for edge caching and DDoS protection, an ALB to distribute traffic across multiple AZs, EC2 instances in at least two AZs for compute redundancy, and RDS for reliable data storage. This architecture survives single AZ failures.

title: Find the Lambda Timeout Root Cause
description: Analyze CloudWatch logs to diagnose why a Lambda function is timing out intermittently.
scenario: A Lambda function processing API requests is intermittently timing out after 30 seconds. Analyze the CloudWatch logs to find the root cause.

logs.message: DynamoDB ProvisionedThroughputExceededException — retrying with exponential backoff

answers.text: Lambda cold start causes the timeout
Token validation is taking too long
DynamoDB table is throttling reads due to exceeded provisioned throughput

explanation: The logs show repeated ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors from DynamoDB with exponential backoff retries. The SDK retries consume the entire 30-second Lambda timeout. The fix is to switch the DynamoDB table to on-demand capacity mode or increase provisioned read capacity units.

title: Debug a Failed API Request
description: Trace a failing HTTPS request through the network path from client to API server to find the broken hop.
scenario: Users report 504 Gateway Timeout errors when calling your API at api.example.com. Trace each hop to find where the request fails.

steps.label: DNS Resolution
steps.detail: Route 53 resolves api.example.com to ALB DNS name correctly.

steps.label: TLS Handshake
steps.detail: ACM certificate is valid. TLS 1.2 handshake succeeds.

steps.label: ALB Security Group
steps.detail: ALB security group allows inbound HTTPS (443) from 0.0.0.0/0.

steps.label: EC2 Security Group
steps.detail: EC2 security group only allows inbound on port 80. ALB target group is configured for port 8080. Port mismatch — traffic is blocked.

steps.label: Application
steps.detail: Application is running and healthy on port 8080.

answers.text: EC2 security group blocks ALB traffic on port 8080

explanation: The EC2 security group allows inbound traffic on port 80, but the ALB target group forwards to port 8080. Since the security group doesn't allow port 8080, the ALB health checks fail and requests time out with 504 errors. The fix is to update the EC2 security group to allow inbound traffic on port 8080 from the ALB security group.

title: Order the Incident Response Steps
description: A security incident has been detected. Put the AWS incident response steps in the correct order.
scenario: GuardDuty has detected unauthorized API calls from compromised IAM credentials. Order the incident response steps correctly.

steps.text: Disable the compromised IAM access keys
Attach a deny-all policy to the compromised user
Review CloudTrail logs for scope of unauthorized activity
Identify and revert any unauthorized changes to resources
Rotate all credentials and create new access keys
Document findings and update security policies

explanation: The correct incident response order is: (1) Immediately disable compromised keys to stop the threat, (2) apply deny-all to prevent any remaining sessions from acting, (3) investigate the scope via CloudTrail, (4) remediate unauthorized changes, (5) issue fresh credentials once containment is confirmed, and (6) document lessons learned. Containment must come before investigation to limit blast radius.

title: Fix ALB Health Check Configuration
description: An ALB is marking all targets as unhealthy. Fix the health check configuration to restore traffic flow.
scenario: Your ALB target group shows all EC2 targets as unhealthy. The application listens on port 8080 at path /api/health and responds with 200. Fix the target group health check configuration.

configItems.label: Health Check Protocol
options: HTTP
HTTPS
TCP
GRPC

explanation: Three settings are wrong: (1) Protocol should be HTTP, not HTTPS — the app does not serve TLS on the backend. (2) Port must match the application port 8080, not the default 80. (3) Path must match the actual health endpoint /api/health. The healthy threshold of 5 is excessive — 2 is standard. Interval and timeout were already correct.

title: Reduce Monthly AWS Spending
description: Optimize an over-provisioned architecture to bring monthly costs under the target budget while maintaining functionality.
scenario: Your team's monthly AWS bill is $2,150. The target budget is $900. Replace over-provisioned services with cost-effective alternatives while maintaining equivalent functionality.
explanation: The optimal strategy brings costs to ~$480/mo: (1) Lambda replaces always-on EC2 instances for an API with variable traffic ($45 vs $520). (2) Aurora Serverless v2 scales to demand instead of a fixed oversized RDS ($350 vs $1200). (3) VPC Endpoints eliminate NAT Gateway data processing fees for AWS service traffic ($20 vs $210). (4) S3 Lifecycle policies automatically move aging data to cheaper tiers ($65 vs $220). Avoid Spot for production APIs (unreliable) and don't sacrifice Multi-AZ for databases (availability risk).

title: Secure an S3-Backed Application
description: Identify and fix security vulnerabilities in an application that stores user data in S3.
scenario: A security audit of your S3-backed application has identified several vulnerabilities. For each issue, select the correct remediation.

issues.issue: Block Public Access is disabled and bucket ACL grants public read
options: Enable S3 Block Public Access (all settings) and remove public ACL grants
Add a bucket policy denying anonymous access
Enable versioning on the bucket
Move bucket to a private VPC endpoint
issues.correctOption: Enable S3 Block Public Access (all settings) and remove public ACL grants

issues.issue: Server-side encryption is not enabled. Objects are stored unencrypted.
options: Enable SSE-S3 (AES-256) as default encryption
Enable SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key and deny unencrypted uploads via bucket policy
Encrypt objects client-side before upload
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
issues.correctOption: Enable SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key and deny unencrypted uploads via bucket policy

issues.issue: Role policy grants s3:* on Resource: * for the entire account
options: Restrict actions to s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject on the specific bucket ARN only
Add a condition key restricting to the current VPC
Add MFA requirement to the policy
Create a service control policy (SCP) to restrict S3 access
issues.correctOption: Restrict actions to s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject on the specific bucket ARN only

issues.issue: No access logging is enabled. Cannot audit who accessed data.
options: Enable CloudTrail S3 data events for the bucket
Enable S3 server access logging to a separate log bucket
Use Amazon Macie to scan for access patterns
Enable VPC Flow Logs
issues.correctOption: Enable CloudTrail S3 data events for the bucket

issues.issue: Versioning is disabled. Accidental deletes or overwrites cannot be recovered.
options: Enable versioning with lifecycle rules for non-current versions
Enable cross-region replication
Take daily snapshots using AWS Backup
Enable MFA Delete on the bucket
issues.correctOption: Enable versioning with lifecycle rules for non-current versions

explanation: The five critical fixes are: (1) Block Public Access prevents accidental exposure — it overrides ACLs and bucket policies. (2) SSE-KMS with a CMK provides encryption plus audit trail via CloudTrail, and the deny policy prevents unencrypted uploads. (3) Least-privilege IAM scopes the role to only needed actions on the specific bucket. (4) CloudTrail S3 data events provide detailed per-object audit logging. (5) Versioning protects against accidental deletes and enables recovery of previous versions.

title: Improve API Response Times
description: Optimize a slow serverless API by selecting the correct performance improvement for each bottleneck.
scenario: Your serverless API (API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB) has a P99 latency of 4.2 seconds. The SLA requires P99 under 500ms. Identify the correct optimization for each performance bottleneck.
architectureDescription: Client → CloudFront (not configured) → API Gateway (REST) → Lambda (1024MB, Python 3.12, no provisioned concurrency) → DynamoDB (on-demand, no caching layer)

problems.problem: First invocation after idle period takes 3-5 seconds due to Python runtime initialization and large deployment package (250MB with ML dependencies).
options: Enable Provisioned Concurrency with at least 5 instances
Increase Lambda memory to 3008MB
Switch to Python 3.13 runtime
Reduce Lambda timeout to 5 seconds
problems.correctOption: Enable Provisioned Concurrency with at least 5 instances

problems.problem: Repeated reads for popular items hit DynamoDB directly every time. Average read latency is 8ms but contributes to aggregate latency under load.
options: Switch to DynamoDB strongly consistent reads
Add DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) cluster for microsecond caching
Increase DynamoDB read capacity units
Enable DynamoDB global tables
problems.correctOption: Add DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator) cluster for microsecond caching

problems.problem: Identical API responses are generated from scratch on every request. Many endpoints return the same data for minutes at a time.
options: Enable API Gateway response caching with appropriate TTL
Switch from REST API to HTTP API
Add a CloudFront distribution in front of API Gateway
Implement Lambda response streaming
problems.correctOption: Enable API Gateway response caching with appropriate TTL

problems.problem: API returns full DynamoDB item attributes even when clients only need 3-4 fields. Average response is 45KB.
options: Enable API Gateway response compression
Use DynamoDB projection expressions and return only needed fields
Switch to DynamoDB Streams for real-time updates
Paginate all responses to 10 items
problems.correctOption: Use DynamoDB projection expressions and return only needed fields

explanation: Four optimizations bring latency under 500ms: (1) Provisioned Concurrency eliminates cold starts — the #1 latency contributor for infrequently invoked functions with large packages. (2) DAX provides microsecond read caching for hot items, reducing DynamoDB round trips. (3) API Gateway caching eliminates Lambda invocations entirely for repeated requests. (4) Projection expressions reduce data transfer and processing by fetching only needed attributes. Together these address cold starts, database access, API layer, and payload size.

title: Write a Cross-Account S3 Read Policy
description: Write an IAM policy that grants read-only access to a specific S3 bucket from a cross-account role.
scenario: Account B (444455556666) needs to read objects from the 'shared-data-bucket' in Account A (111122223333). Write an IAM policy for the role in Account B that follows least-privilege.
requirements: Allow s3:GetObject on objects in shared-data-bucket only
Allow s3:ListBucket on the shared-data-bucket only
Deny access to any other bucket

testCases.description: Put object in shared bucket (should be denied)
Delete object from shared bucket (should be denied)
Read from a different bucket (should be denied)
List a different bucket (should be denied)

explanation: The correct policy has two statements: (1) Allow s3:GetObject on 'arn:aws:s3:::shared-data-bucket/*' for object-level access. (2) Allow s3:ListBucket on 'arn:aws:s3:::shared-data-bucket' (bucket-level ARN without /*). No wildcard actions or resources — only the specific actions and bucket needed. The initial policy with s3:* and Resource:* violates least-privilege and would fail the Deny test cases.

title: Handle a Traffic Spike
description: A 10x traffic spike is overwhelming your infrastructure. Select the correct scaling action for each metric.
scenario: Black Friday traffic has spiked 10x. Multiple services are hitting their limits. For each critical metric, choose the correct scaling action to stabilize the system.

options: Increase ASG max capacity to 50 and set target tracking to 60% CPU
Switch all instances to c5.4xlarge
Add a second ASG in a different region
Enable EC2 instance store caching
metrics.correctOption: Increase ASG max capacity to 50 and set target tracking to 60% CPU

options: Request concurrency limit increase and set reserved concurrency for critical functions
Reduce Lambda timeout to free up concurrency
Switch Lambda to ARM64 architecture
Enable Lambda Provisioned Concurrency for all functions
metrics.correctOption: Request concurrency limit increase and set reserved concurrency for critical functions

options: Switch to on-demand capacity mode for automatic scaling
Add a GSI to distribute writes
Enable DynamoDB Streams
Increase provisioned WCU to 80,000
metrics.correctOption: Switch to on-demand capacity mode for automatic scaling

options: Increase consumer Lambda batch size and concurrency
Switch to SQS FIFO queue
Increase message visibility timeout to 1 hour
Delete old messages from the queue
metrics.correctOption: Increase consumer Lambda batch size and concurrency

options: Request API Gateway account-level throttle increase via AWS Support
Switch from REST API to WebSocket API
Enable API Gateway caching
Add CloudFront in front of API Gateway
metrics.correctOption: Request API Gateway account-level throttle increase via AWS Support

explanation: The correct actions: (1) Increase ASG max capacity — the current limit prevents scaling out. Target tracking at 60% CPU provides headroom. (2) Request Lambda concurrency increase — the account-level limit must be raised via AWS Support, and reserved concurrency protects critical functions from noisy neighbors. (3) DynamoDB on-demand mode auto-scales to traffic without pre-provisioning. (4) Increasing Lambda batch size and concurrency for SQS consumers processes more messages per invocation. (5) API Gateway account-level throttle must be raised via Support — caching helps but doesn't solve a hard limit issue.
